# Dare You Fight {.hero-title}
## W.E.B. Du Bois in <span class="crisis-title">The Crisis</span> {.hero-subtitle}
:::

"A toothache is agitation," Du Bois [wrote in November 1910](Volumes/01/01/Agitation.html), answering critics who urged silence. "Is a toothache a good thing? No. Is it therefore useless? No. It is supremely useful, for it tells the body of decay, dyspepsia and death." For twenty-four years he made <span class="crisis-title">The Crisis</span> the toothache of American democracy: documenting lynching, tracking disfranchisement, connecting Jim Crow to empire, and building the case for Black citizenship in prose that could shift from forensic precision to prophetic fury within a single page.

This archive collects over 700 of those editorials, spanning the magazine's founding in 1910 through Du Bois's resignation in 1934. They can be [browsed by theme](browse.qmd), [read chronologically](listing.qmd), or [explored by similarity](map.html).

---

## Where to Start

::::: {.grid .featured-grid}

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .featured-card}
### [Agitation](Volumes/01/01/Agitation.html) {.featured-title}
<span class="featured-date">November 1910</span>

The editorial posture from the first issue. Du Bois declares what <span class="crisis-title">The Crisis</span> will be and why silence is not an option.
::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .featured-card}
### [Returning Soldiers](Volumes/18/01/returning_soldiers.html) {.featured-title}
<span class="featured-date">May 1919</span>

"We *return*. We *return from fighting*. We *return fighting*." The moment the patriotic compact breaks, in the issue that sold 106,000 copies.
::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .featured-card}
### [Criteria of Negro Art](Volumes/32/06/criteria_of_negro_art.html) {.featured-title}
<span class="featured-date">October 1926</span>

"All Art is propaganda and ever must be." Du Bois's philosophy of art, politics, and the duty Black artists owe the community that produced them.
::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .featured-card}
### [On Being Crazy](Volumes/26/01/on_being_crazy.html) {.featured-title}
<span class="featured-date">June 1923</span>

A Socratic dialogue on the absurdity of segregation. Fiction as weapon, anticipating the literature of the absurd by decades.
::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .featured-card}
### [The Princess of the Hither Isles](Volumes/06/06/princess_of_hither_isles.html) {.featured-title}
<span class="featured-date">November 1913</span>

Allegorical fable compressing the history of racial exploitation into a story about a princess and a tower of gold. A different Du Bois.
::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .featured-card}
### [Segregation](Volumes/41/01/segregation.html) {.featured-title}
<span class="featured-date">January 1934</span>

The editorial that ended his editorship. Du Bois argues the unthinkable: the segregated must build within the system they oppose.
::::

:::::
